original_question: Let an abelian square be a factor uv of a finite word such that u and v have the same Parikh vector, and let two abelian squares be considered distinct when they are different factor strings. Suppose a word of length n over an arbitrary alphabet contains k distinct abelian square factors. Must there always exist a binary word of the same length n that contains at least k distinct abelian square factors?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 0.1 in the opening section "The maximum number of abelian squares in a linear word" (the paper’s quoted Fici-Mignosi conjecture about larger alphabets not beating binary for distinct abelian-square factors).
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right object and almost the exact intent of the paper: it uses the Parikh-vector definition of abelian square, counts distinct abelian-square factors as different factor strings rather than occurrences or Parikh classes, fixes the word length n, allows an arbitrary alphabet for the original word, and asks whether a binary word of the same length can always match or exceed that count. This is precisely the conjectural comparison the paper states in its section on the maximum number of abelian squares in linear words.
missing_details: The paper’s ambient setting is finite linear words; this should be stated explicitly so the question is not confused with circular words, which are treated separately later in the paper.
A factor should be made explicit as a contiguous subword.
The abelian-square factors being counted should be understood as nonempty abelian squares (equivalently, factors uv with |u|=|v|>0 and equal Parikh vectors).

The paper states the conjecture informally with the word "many"; to make it stand-alone and mathematically sharp, the universal quantifier should be made explicit: for every n and every word of length n, there exists a binary word of length n with at least as many distinct abelian-square factors.

It helps to say explicitly that the count is by distinct factor strings, not by multiplicity of occurrence and not by equivalence classes of Parikh vectors, since the paper distinguishes distinct abelian squares from equivalent/non-equivalent ones in the preliminaries.
refined_question: For every integer n >= 1, is the following true? If w is a finite linear word of length n over an arbitrary finite alphabet, then there exists a binary word b of length n such that b has at least as many distinct nonempty abelian-square factors as w. Here a factor means a contiguous subword, and an abelian square is a factor uv with |u|=|v|>0 and u and v having the same Parikh vector; two abelian-square factors are counted as distinct when they are different words.
justification: The draft is targeting the paper’s opening conjecture on the maximum number of distinct abelian squares in linear words. In the preliminaries, the paper defines abelian squares via Parikh vectors and explicitly distinguishes distinct abelian squares from equivalent ones. Immediately afterward, in the section on maximum numbers for linear words, the author says that increasing the alphabet size likely does not increase the maximum number of abelian squares and then states Conjecture 0.1: if a word of length n contains many distinct abelian-square factors, then there exists a binary word of length n containing at least as many distinct abelian-square factors. Your draft already sharpens the paper’s informal "many" into the correct quantified comparison; the only real additions needed are the linear-word setting, contiguity of factors, and the nonempty-factor convention.
